readings.c1s1:
¶
'''through-going''' (thrö′gō″ing), ''n.'' [Cf. ''thorough-go.''] A scolding; a severe reprimand or reproof. ''Scott,'' Rob Roy, xiv. [Scotch.]

'''through-going''' (thrö′gō″ing), ''a.'' [Also ''through-gaun;'' cf. ''thorough-going.''] Thorough-going; active; energetic; stirring; bustling. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|She seems to be a plump and jocose little woman; gleg, blythe, and ''through-gaun'' for her years.
{{right|''Blackwood's Mag.,'' VIII. 265.}}}}

'''through-handling†''', ''n.'' Active management.

{{smaller block|The king . . . (but skiming anything that came before him) was disciplined to leave the ''throug[h]-handling'' of all to his gentle wife. ''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, p. 177. (''Davies.'')}}

'''through-lighted''' (thrö′lī″ted), ''a.'' Lighted by windows or other openings placed on opposite sides.

{{smaller block|Not only rooms windowed on both ends, called ''through-lighted,'' but with two or more windows on the same side, are enemies to this art.
{{right|''Sir H. Wotton,'' Elements of Architecture.}}}}

'''throughly†''' (thrö′li), ''adv.'' [ME. ''throughely;'' < ''through''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''thoroughly.''] 1. Completely; wholly; thoroughly.

{{smaller block|"Therfore," quod she, "I prae yow feithfully
That ye will do the pleasure that ye may
Onto my sone, and teche hym ''throughely''
That att longith to hym to do or saye."
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 346.}}}}

{{smaller block|The night, ''throughly'' spent in these mixed matters, was for that time banished the face of the earth.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, v.}}}}

{{smaller block|It hath deserved it
''Throughly'' and ''throughly.''
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Volpone, i. 1.}}}}

2. Without reserve; thoroughly; carefully; earnestly.

¶
'''through-paced†''' (thrö′pāst), ''a.'' Thorough-paced.

'''through-stitch†''' (thrö′stich), ''adv.'' [Also ''thorough-stitch.''] To completion; to the very end.

{{smaller block|He that threads his needle with the sharp eyes of industry shall in time go ''through-stitch'' with the new suit of preferment.
{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, ii. 3.}}
The taylers hell, who indeed are accounted the best bread men in the ship, and such as goe ''through stitch'' with what they take in hand.
{{right|''John Taylor'', Works (1630). (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''through-stone''' (thrö′stōn), ''n.'' [< ''through''<sup>1</sup> + ''stone.''] In ''arch.'', a bonder or bond-stone; a stone placed across the breadth of a wall, so that one end appears in each face of the wall, as distinguished from a stone of which the greatest length is placed in the direction of the course of the wall; a perpend. Also ''thorough-stone.''

{{smaller block|Od, he is not stirring yet, mair than he were a ''through-stane!''
{{right|''Scott'', Monastery, Int. Ep.}}}}

'''throughtly†''', ''adv.'' Same as ''throughout.''

'''throupe†''', ''n.'' Same as ''thrope.''

'''throve''' (thrōv). Preterit of ''thrive.''

'''throw<sup>1</sup>''' (thrō), ''v.''; pret. ''threw'', pp. ''thrown'', ppr. ''throwing.'' [Sc. also ''thraw;'' < ME. ''throwen, thrawen'' (pret. ''threw'', pp. ''throwen, thrawen''), < AS. ''thrāwan'' (pret. ''threów'', pp. ''thrāwen''), turn, twist, = D. ''draaijen'' = MLG. ''dreien, dreigen'', LG. ''draien, dreien'', turn (in a lathe), = OHG. ''drāhan, drājan'', MHG. ''drǣjen, drǣn'', G. ''drehen''

Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 65.}}}} {{smaller block|Truly and ''throughly'' to live up to the principles of their religion.{{right|''Tillotson.''}}}} '''through-mortise''' (thrö′môr″tis), ''n.'' A mortise which passes entirely through the timber in which it is made. '''throughout''' (thrö-out′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ''through''1 + ''out.'' Cf. ''thoroughout.''] '''I.''' ''adv.'' Everywhere; in every part; in all respects. {{smaller block|His youth and age, All of a piece ''throughout'', and all divine. ''Dryden.''}} {{smaller block|His conduct ''throughout'' was equally defective in principle and in sound policy.{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 1.}}}} '''II.''' ''prep.'' Quite through; from one end or side of to the other; in every part of. {{smaller block|There is not that thing in the world of more grave and urgent importance ''throughout'' the whole life of man, then is discipline.{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|''Meer.'' The thing is for recovery of drowned land. . . . ''Eng. Thoroughout'' England.{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The conflict lasted ''throughout'' the night, with carnage on both sides.{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 60.}}}} '''throughoutly†''' (thrö-out′li), ''adv.'' E. T. S.), l. 3075.}}}} {{smaller block|If this first worke bee throughly and ''throughoutly'' dispatched, as I hope it is, the great Remora is removed.{{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 36.}}}} '''through-paced†''' (thrö′pāst), ''a.'' Thorough-paced. '''through-stitch†''' (thrö′stich), ''adv.'' (''Nares.'')}}}} '''through-stone''' (thrö′stōn), ''n.'' [< ''through''1 + ''stone.''] In ''arch.'', a bonder or bond-stone; a stone placed across the breadth of a wall, so that one end appears in each face of the wall, as distinguished from a stone of which the greatest length is placed in the direction of the course of the wall; a perpend. Also ''thorough-stone.'' {{smaller block|Od, he is not stirring yet, mair than he were a ''through-stane!'' {{right|''Scott'', Monastery, Int. Ep.}}}} '''throughtly†''', ''adv.'' Same as ''throughout.'' '''throupe†''', ''n.'' Same as ''thrope.'' '''throve''' (thrōv). Preterit of ''thrive.'' '''throw1''' (thrō), ''v.''; pret. ''threw'', pp. ''thrown'', ppr. ''throwing.'' [Sc. also ''thraw;'' < ME. ''throwen, thrawen'' (pret. ''threw'', pp. ''throwen, thrawen''), < AS. ''thrāwan'' (pret. ''threów'', pp. ''thrāwen''), turn, twist, = D. ''draaijen'' = MLG. ''dreien, dreigen'', LG. ''draien, dreien'', turn (in a lathe), = OHG. ''drāhan, drājan'', MHG. ''drǣjen, drǣn'', G. ''drehen'' = Sw. ''dreja'' = Dan. ''dreje'' = Goth. *''thraian'' (not recorded), turn. Hence ult. ''thread''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To turn; twist; specifically, to form into threads by twisting two or more filaments together, or by twisting two or more singles together in a direction contrary to the twist of the singles themselves: as, to ''throw'' silk: sometimes applied in a wide sense to the whole series of operations by which silk is prepared for the weaver. {{smaller block|The art of spinning and ''throwing'' silk had been introduced [into England in 1455] by a company of silk women, of what country is not known. {{right|''A. Barlow'', Weaving, p. 18.}}}} '''2.''' To shape on a potters' wheel. {{smaller|The mass of clay revolves under the hands of the potter, who gives it the desired form. See ''thrown ware'', under ''thrown''.}} '''3'''†. To fashion by turning on a lathe; turn.— '''4.''' To cast; heave; pitch; toss; fling: literally or figuratively: as, to ''throw'' a stone at a bird. {{smaller block|Sothely the boot in the mydil see was ''throwen'' with waiwis, forsothe the wynd was contrarie. {{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. xiv. 24.}} ''Throw'' physic to the dogs; I'll none of it. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 3. 47.}} This day was the sayd Anthonie Gelber sowed in a Chauina filled with stones, and ''throwen'' into the sea. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', II. 110.}} Scurrility! That is he that ''throweth'' scandals— Soweth and ''throweth'' scandals, as 'twere dirt, Even in the face of holiness and devotion. {{right|''Randolph'', Muses' Looking Glass, iv. 5.}} The contempt he ''throws'' upon them in another passage is yet more remarkable. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 135.}}}} '''5.''' To cast with sudden force or violence; impel violently; hurl; dash: as, the shock ''threw'' the wall down. {{smaller block|What tempest, I trow, ''threw'' this whale . . . ashore at Windsor? {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 1. 65.}}}} {{smaller block|Each sudden passion ''throws'' me where it lists,
And overwhelms all that oppose my will. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 4.}}}} 6. To fling; floor; give a fall to, as in wrestling; unhorse, as in justing. {{smaller block|Charles in a moment ''threw'' him, and broke three of his ribs. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2. 135.}}}} 7. To unseat and bring to the ground. {{smaller block|If a nag is to ''throw'' me, I say, let him have some blood. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xx.}}}} 8. To cast; shed. {{smaller block|There the snake ''throws'' her enamell'd skin. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., ii. 1. 255.}}}} 9. To spread or put on carelessly or hurriedly: as, to ''throw'' a shawl over one's shoulders. {{smaller block|I have seen her . . . ''throw'' her nightgown upon her. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 1. 5.}}}} 10. To advance or place quickly, as by some rapid movement. {{smaller block|It would not be possible for Pemberton to attack me with all his troops at one place, and I determined to ''throw'' my army between his and fight him in detail. {{right|''U. S. Grant'', Personal Memoirs, I. 496.}}}} 11. To bring forth; produce, as young; bear; cast: said especially of rabbits. {{smaller block|When a pure race of white or black pigeons ''throws'' a slaty-blue bird . . . we are quite unable to assign any proximate cause. {{right|''Darwin.''}}}} {{smaller block|Mares that have done much hard work are not the best dams that can be selected, as they are apt to slip their foals, or to ''throw'' undersized ones. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XII. 188.}}}} 12. To make a cast with, as dice; play with, as dice; make (a cast of dice). {{smaller block|Set less than thou ''throwest.''{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 136.}}}} {{smaller block|That great day of expense, in which a man is to ''throw'' his last cast for an eternity of joys or sorrows.{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 533.}}}} 13. In ''card-playing'', to lay upon the table; play, as a card.—14. To turn; direct; cast: as, to ''throw'' one's eyes to the ground. {{smaller block|Lo, what befel! he ''threw'' his eye aside.{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 3. 103.}}}} 15. To sell, as a race or game; allow another to win unnecessarily or in accordance with previous agreement.—{{smaller|'''Throw up''', in ''printing'', a direction to enlarge the size of a line of displayed type.—'''To throw across''', to construct across: as, to ''throw'' a bridge ''across'' a river.—'''To throw a levant†.''' See ''levant''3.—'''To throw a sop to Cerberus.''' See ''sop''.—'''To throw away.''' (''a'') To cast from one's hand; put suddenly out of one's hold or possession.}} {{smaller block|The Duke took out the Knife, and ''threw'' it ''away.''{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 7.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') To part with without compensation; give or spend recklessly; squander; lose by negligence or folly; waste.}} {{smaller block|Dilatory fortune plays the jilt With the brave, noble, honest, gallant man, To ''throw'' herself ''away'' on fools and knaves.{{right|''Otway'', The Orphan, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|She ''threw away'' her money upon roaring bullies, that went about the streets.{{right|''Arbuthnot'', Hist. John Bull.}}}} {{smaller block|It is bare justice to Clive to say that, proud and overbearing as he was, kindness was never ''thrown away'' upon him.{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Clive.}}}} (c) To reject; refuse; lose by indifference or neglect: as, to ''throw away'' a good offer.—'''To throw back.''' (''a'') To reflect, as light, etc. (''b'') To reject; refuse. (''c'') To cast back, as a slur or an insinuation.—'''To throw by,''' to cast or lay aside as useless; discard. {{smaller block|It can but shew
Like one of Juno's disguises; and
When things succeed be ''thrown by'', or let fall. {{right|''B. Jonson.'' (''Johnson.'')}}}} '''To throw cold water on.''' See ''cold.''—'''To throw down.''' (''a'') To cast to the ground or other lower position: as, the men ''threw down'' their tools. See ''to throw down the gauntlet'', under ''gauntlet''1. {{smaller block|That with which K. Richard was charged, beside the Wrong done to Leopold in ''throwing down'' his Colours at Ptolemais, was the Death of Conrade Duke of Tyre. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 64.}}}} (''b'') To bring from an erect or exalted to a prostrate position or condition; hence, to overturn; subvert; demolish; destroy. {{smaller block|Must one rash word, the infirmity of age,
''Throw down'' the merit of my better years? {{right|''Addison'', Cato, ii. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|In January 1740 they had three great shocks of an earthquake immediately after one another, which ''threw down'' some mosques and several houses. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 195.}}}} '''To throw dust in one's eyes.''' See ''dust''1.—'''To throw in.''' (''a'') To cast or place within; insert; inject, as a fluid. (''b'') To put in or deposit along with another or others: as, he has ''thrown in'' his fortune with yours. {{smaller block|We cannot ''throw in'' our lot with revolutionaries and with those who are guilty of treason to the Constitution and to the Empire. {{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXV. 303.}}}} (''c'') To interpolate: as, he ''threw in'' a word now and then. (''d'') To add without reckoning, or as if to complete or effect a bargain or sale: as, I will ''throw in'' this book if you buy the lot.—'''To throw into shape,''' to give form or arrangement to. {{smaller block|It would be well to ''throw'' his notes and materials ''into'' some ''shape.'' {{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), Int., p. xii.}}}} '''To throw into the bargain.''' Same as ''to throw in'' (''d''). —'''To throw light on,''' to make clear or intelligible. {{smaller block|Lady Sarah Cowper has left a memorandum respecting her father, Lord Cowper, which ''throws light on'' this subject. {{right|''J. Ashton,'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, II. 141.}}}} '''To throw off.''' (''a'') To cast off, away, or aside; divest one's self of hurriedly or carelessly; abandon the use of; free one's self of, as an impediment; get rid of, as a disease: as, to ''throw off'' one's clothes; to ''throw off'' all disguise; to ''throw off'' a cold or a fever. {{smaller block|The free spirit of mankind at length ''Throws'' its last fetters ''off.'' {{right|''Bryant,'' The Ages.}}}} {{smaller block|An eschar was formed, which was soon ''thrown off,'' leaving a healthy granulating surface. {{right|''J. M. Carnochan,'' Operative Surgery, p. 46.}}}} (''b'') To discard; dismiss: as, to ''throw off'' an acquaintance or a dependent. (''c'') To do or say in a rapid offhand manner: as, to ''throw off'' a poem. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|Often Addison's most brilliant efforts are built upon a chance hint ''thrown off'' at random by Steele's hurrying pen. {{right|''A. Dobson,'' Int. to Steele, p. xxx.}}}} '''To throw on,''' to put on or don hastily or carelessly: as, he ''threw on'' his cloak.—'''To throw one's self down,''' to lie down.—'''To throw one's self into,''' to engage heartily, earnestly, or vigorously in: as, he ''threw himself into'' the contest, and did good service.—'''To throw one's self on''' or '''upon,''' to cast one's faith or confidence upon; trust or resign one's self to, as for favor or protection; repose upon: as, to ''throw one's self on'' the mercy of the court. {{smaller block|In time of temptation be not busy to dispute, but . . . ''throw yourself upon'' God. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Holy Living, iv. 1.}} '''To throw open.''' (''a'') To open suddenly or widely. {{smaller block|"Who knocks?" cried Goodman Garvin. The door was ''open thrown.'' {{right|''Whittier,'' Mary Garvin.}}}} (''b'') To give free or unrestricted access to; remove all barriers, obstacles, or restrictions from: as, the appointment was ''thrown open'' to public competition.—'''To throw open the door to.''' See ''door.''—'''To throw out.''' (''a'') To cast out; expel; reject or discard. {{smaller block|Admit that Monarchy of itself may be convenient to som Nations; yet to us who have ''thrown'' it ''out'', receiv'd back again, it cannot but prove pernicious. {{right|''Milton'', Free Commonwealth.}}}} (''b'') To cause to project, or to become prominent; build out: as, to ''throw out'' a pier or landing-stage, or a wing of a building. (''c'') To emit: as, that lamp ''throws out'' a bright light. (''d'') To give utterance to; insinuate: as, to ''throw out'' a hint. {{smaller block|I have ''thrown out'' words That would have fetch'd warm blood upon the cheeks Of guilty men, and he is never mov'd. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid's Tragedy, iv. 2.}}}} (''e'') To put off the right track; confuse; embarrass: as, interruption ''throws'' one ''out''. (''f'') To leave behind; distance: as, a horse ''thrown'' completely ''out'' of the race. (''g'') To reject; exclude: as, the bill was ''thrown out'' on the second reading. (''h'') In ''printing'', to reject or throw aside, as printed sheets that are imperfect. (''i'') In ''base-ball'', to put out, as a base-runner, by a ball fielded to one of the players on or near a base. (''j'') In ''cricket'', to put out (a batsman) when he is out of his ground by a fielder hitting the wicket.—'''To throw over,''' to desert; abandon; neglect. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|They say the Rads are going to ''throw'' us ''over''. {{right|''Disraeli'', Coningsby.}}}} {{smaller block|Saddled with a vast number of engagements, any of which (and this made him none the less popular) he was ready to ''throw over'' at a moment's notice. {{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, II. xi.}}}}
